content_voiceover: These questions dig into two modern aspects of inhibitor management. The first asks about the criteria for stopping immune tolerance induction, or ITI, successfully in a two year old with severe hemophilia A and a moderate titer inhibitor of eight point four Bethesda units. Success is defined by three things together, a persistently negative inhibitor titer under zero point six Bethesda units, factor eight recovery greater than sixty six percent of expected, not less than or equal to as one distractor suggests, and a factor eight half life of at least six hours. There's no fixed rule that ITI must run less than thirty three months, so that answer choice is the one that doesn't belong among true success criteria. The second question moves into real world practice with emicizumab, a bispecific antibody used for prophylaxis in patients with high responding inhibitors. Here a five year old on emicizumab prophylaxis has an acute traumatic knee bleed. Because emicizumab only provides partial, steady state hemostatic support and is not itself a rescue treatment for acute bleeding, the first line approach for a breakthrough bleed in an inhibitor patient is still a bypassing agent, in this case a weight based dose of activated prothrombin complex concentrate, while being mindful of thrombotic risk if aPCC is combined with emicizumab at high doses.
keypoints: Successful ITI requires negative titer under 0.6 BU, FVIII recovery over 66%, and half-life at least 6 hours
No fixed time limit like under 33 months defines ITI success
Emicizumab is prophylaxis, not acute bleed treatment
Acute breakthrough bleeds on emicizumab still need a bypassing agent like APCC
Watch for thrombotic risk when combining high-dose APCC with emicizumab
keypoint_voiceover: Two practical rules to lock in. Successful immune tolerance induction means all three criteria together, negative inhibitor titer, factor eight recovery over sixty six percent, and half life of at least six hours, there is no fixed treatment duration cutoff. And separately, emicizumab covers baseline prophylaxis but does not treat an acute bleed by itself, so breakthrough bleeding in an inhibitor patient on emicizumab still calls for a bypassing agent like activated prothrombin complex concentrate, dosed carefully because combining it with emicizumab raises thrombotic risk.
